# Abstract {.unnumbered}

**Background:** Adults with disability tend to need more healthcare and to have less capacity to pay for it. Kenya replaced the National Hospital Insurance Fund with the Social Health Authority (SHA) in October 2024, so KDHS 2022 is the last nationally representative measurement before that transition.

**Methods:** Cross-sectional analysis of the KDHS 2022 person recode file, restricted to adults aged 18 years and above in the long-questionnaire subsample, where the disability, insurance and service-use modules were administered. Disability was measured with the Washington Group Short Set (WG-SS). We estimated survey-weighted prevalences and prevalence ratios from quasi-Poisson models under three adjustment sets with marginal standardised differences; adjacent severity categories were contrasted directly. Amounts paid and payer sources were analysed among those who paid.

**Results:** Of `r fmt_count(key_results$sample_long_questionnaire)` adults, `r fmt_pct_point_only(key_results$wg_disability)` met the WG threshold. Uninsured prevalence was higher among them unadjusted (`r fmt_contrast_apr("uninsured", "crude")`) and after adjustment for sex, age group and residence (`r fmt_contrast_apr("uninsured", "confounder")`; standardised difference `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * key_results$contrast("uninsured", "confounder")$standardised_difference)` percentage points), but null once wealth and education were added (`r fmt_contrast_apr("uninsured", "full")`). Outpatient use and hospitalisation were higher in every specification (fully adjusted PR `r fmt_contrast_apr_short("outpatient_last4w", "full")` and `r fmt_contrast_apr_short("inpatient_last12m", "full")`). Among outpatient users with disability, `r fmt_pct_point_only(key_results$disability_payment)` paid something, insured or not (`r fmt_pct_point_only(key_results$disability_payment_insured)` and `r fmt_pct_point_only(key_results$disability_payment_uninsured)`). Among those who paid, an insurer met any part of the bill for `r fmt_pct_row_point(key_results$payer_source_summary, "WG disability, insured")` of insured adults with disability, whose median cash payment was KSh `r fmt_money_row("WG disability, insured", "cash_median")` against KSh `r fmt_money_row("WG disability, uninsured", "cash_median")` for uninsured adults with disability.

**Conclusions:** The crude coverage deficit among adults with disability was explained statistically by their older, poorer and less educated composition; their higher use of care was not. At the point of care, holding cover rarely meant that an insurer paid. Monitoring enrolment counts alone would miss both.

**Keywords:** disability; Washington Group Short Set; health insurance; out-of-pocket payment; care-seeking; health equity; Kenya; demographic and health survey; universal health coverage; Social Health Authority

# Background

Disability is an under-measured dimension of health-system inequity. The World Health Organization estimates that about 1.3 billion people, roughly 16% of the world's population, live with significant disability, and that barriers to care are steepest in low- and middle-income countries [@who2023disability]. The financing implication is direct: adults with disability tend to need more care, while the same functional difficulty constrains schooling, earnings and the ability to pay a contributory premium.

Kenyan evidence has established that insurance coverage is socially patterned and pro-rich. Analyses of earlier KDHS rounds documented large differences by wealth, education and employment [@kimani2014; @kazungu2017], and a 36-country analysis found the same pattern wherever contributory mechanisms dominate [@barasa2021]. Two analyses of KDHS 2022 itself are already in print: one reports coverage levels and their determinants without examining disability [@alhajeri2026], and one uses coarsened exact matching to separate gross healthcare expenditure from net out-of-pocket payment after reimbursement [@okova2026]. Qualitative work with women with disabilities living in poverty in Kenya has shown that pro-poor financing policies can reach the enrolment margin and still leave people paying [@kabia2018]. What is missing is a national, adult, disability-stratified account that places coverage, care-seeking and payment in one sample.

The policy context has since changed. The Social Health Insurance Act 2023 repealed the NHIF Act and established the Social Health Authority together with three funds: the Primary Healthcare Fund, the Social Health Insurance Fund and the Emergency, Chronic and Critical Illness Fund [@kenya2023sha]. The Act does not create a disability-specific fund or a standing premium exemption for disability. It defines a person with disability who is wholly dependent on and living with a contributor as a beneficiary, includes persons with disability among vulnerable persons, and provides that contributions for households identified as unable to pay, through a means-testing instrument, are met from funds appropriated by Parliament [@kenya2023sha; @kenya2024shiregs]. Eligibility for that support therefore runs through household means testing and administrative identification, not through a functional-difficulty score. The separate legal architecture for disability certification, formerly the Persons with Disabilities Act 2003, was replaced by the Persons with Disabilities Act 2025, in force from 27 May 2025 [@kenya2003pda; @kenya2025pda]. KDHS 2022 records neither certification status nor programme enrolment, so this study cannot speak to who would qualify for public support under either instrument.

KDHS 2022 carries the Washington Group Short Set (WG-SS) in the person recode file, which allows functional difficulty to be measured consistently alongside insurance, service use and payment [@kdhs2022report; @washingtongroup2016]. This study is descriptive and estimates, for Kenyan adults immediately before the SHA transition: (i) the difference in insurance coverage, outpatient use and hospitalisation between adults at and below the WG disability threshold, both unadjusted and under prespecified adjustment sets; (ii) whether coverage varies across WG severity categories once those categories are contrasted formally rather than compared by eye; and (iii) what was paid at the last outpatient visit, how much, and who met the bill. No causal effect of disability or of insurance is estimated.

# Methods

## Study design and data source

This study is reported in accordance with the STROBE statement for cross-sectional studies.

KDHS 2022 used a stratified two-stage cluster design: enumeration areas were selected in the first stage and households within them in the second [@kdhs2022report]. Within each cluster the sampled households were divided between two instruments: one in every two households received the full household questionnaire and the remainder a short version. The disability, insurance, service-use and expenditure modules analysed here were administered only in the full-questionnaire households, so the analytic base is that half-sample. All analyses use the person recode (PR) file, which holds one record per household member.

The household questionnaire is answered by a household respondent on behalf of household members. The disability, insurance, utilisation and payment items used here are therefore household-reported and, for most adults in the file, proxy-reported rather than self-reported. The PR file does not identify which member supplied the information for which record.

## Study population

The analytic population was adult usual residents aged 18 years and above in long-questionnaire households with complete six-domain WG-SS data. The age threshold of 18 was set a priori to match the adult policy population for premium contribution, rather than the 15-year threshold used in the KDHS report tables. Participant flow from the raw file to each outcome-specific denominator is given in Table S1, and missing values by variable in Table S2. Analyses are complete-case within each outcome and model.

## Variables

### Disability

The WG-SS comprises six functional-difficulty items, captured in KDHS 2022 as seeing (`hdis2`), hearing (`hdis4`), communication in the respondent's usual language (`hdis5`), remembering or concentrating (`hdis6`), walking or climbing steps (`hdis7`) and self-care (`hdis8`) [@washingtongroup2016]. The adjacent variables `hdis1` and `hdis3`, which in the standard recode carry use of glasses and of hearing aids, are empty in this dataset and were not used; the seeing and hearing items were therefore analysed as recorded, without information on whether the respondent was assessed with usual assistive devices. The WG threshold was defined as "a lot of difficulty" or "cannot do at all" in at least one domain.

Severity was taken from `hdis9`, the highest degree of difficulty reported across the six domains, and labelled no, mild, moderate and severe functional difficulty. This is a maximum, not a scale: one severe domain and substantial difficulty in several domains are collapsed differently by it. The count of domains at or above threshold is therefore analysed as a prespecified alternative specification.

### Insurance, service use and payment

Insurance coverage was taken from `sh27`, an individual-level item recorded for each household member within the household questionnaire, and NHIF coverage from `sh28a`. Uninsured status was defined as a "no" response; the 293 adults answering "don't know" were treated as missing in the main analysis and grouped with the uninsured in a prespecified sensitivity analysis. Outpatient use in the previous four weeks came from `sh31` and hospitalisation in the previous 12 months from `sh29`.

Payment was measured at three levels. Whether any money was paid at the last outpatient visit came from `sh32`, which is an incidence measure and says nothing about magnitude. The amount came from `sh304`, the total cost of that visit, and the payer split from `sh305a` to `sh305e`, the amounts met in cash, by NHIF, by private insurance, in kind and by other means. The questionnaire asks the amount items only of respondents who reported paying, so the amount analyses are conditional on having paid and are reported as such. Values coded 999998 and above are non-response codes and were set to missing. The gross cost (`sh304`) is distinguished throughout from the cash amount (`sh305a`), which is the net out-of-pocket payment once any insurer contribution is deducted, following the gross-versus-net distinction drawn for these data elsewhere [@okova2026]. KDHS does not collect household consumption or income, so catastrophic and impoverishing health expenditure cannot be constructed from this file, and no such measure is reported.

### Covariates and their assumed roles

Sex, age group (18-29, 30-44, 45-59, 60+) and place of residence (`hv025`) were treated as confounders of the disability contrast: they are fixed or precede functional difficulty in adulthood. Wealth quintile (`hv270`) and educational attainment (`hv106`) were treated as plausible mediators rather than confounders. For a population whose functional difficulty is largely lifelong or acquired well before the survey, disability restricts schooling and earning capacity, which then determine the ability to pay a contributory premium; conditioning on them estimates an association net of that pathway and not a better-confounded total association. Both roles are reported side by side rather than one being chosen. County (`hv024`) was not entered in the models: the long-questionnaire subsample is not powered for 47-county fixed effects in the disability stratum, and no county-level estimates are reported.

## Statistical analysis

All estimates used the complex design: PSU (`hv021`), stratum (`hv022`) and household-member weight (`hv005`/1,000,000), with `nest = TRUE`. The analytic base contains `r fmt_count(key_results$design_metadata$psu_n)` PSUs in `r key_results$design_metadata$strata_n` strata, giving `r fmt_count(key_results$design_metadata$design_df)` design degrees of freedom. Strata containing a single PSU were handled with the centring adjustment (`options(survey.lonely.psu = "adjust")`). Confidence intervals for proportions were logit-transformed, which keeps small-domain intervals inside the unit interval; intervals for regression coefficients use the survey degrees of freedom rather than a normal approximation.

Prevalence ratios were estimated with survey-weighted quasi-Poisson models with a log link, which is appropriate where the outcome is common [@zou2004]. For each of the three whole-sample outcomes we fitted the crude model, a confounder-adjusted model (sex, age group, residence) and a fully adjusted model adding wealth and education, and report both the prevalence ratio and the marginal standardised difference in percentage points, computed by g-computation over the covariate distribution of the analytic sample with delta-method confidence limits.

Severity was tested with prespecified contrasts between adjacent categories, estimated on the linear predictor and exponentiated, together with a design-based global Wald test of the severity term. Overlapping confidence intervals were not used as a test, and no equivalence claim is made, since no equivalence margin was prespecified.

Amounts paid were summarised as survey-weighted medians and means with confidence intervals, and modelled as ratios of geometric means using a survey-weighted linear model on the log amount, given the strong right skew. The payer split was summarised as the proportion of payers for whom an insurer met any part of the bill and as the mean cash share of the reported amounts.

Two analyses condition on having used outpatient care or on having paid. Because disability, insurance, wealth and need all influence care-seeking, these are descriptive associations among the selected group and are not interpretable as effects of insurance; this is stated wherever they are reported.

Prespecified sensitivity analyses covered the coding of "don't know" insurance responses, the multi-domain alternative to the severity summary, and a comparison of adults included in and excluded from the fully adjusted model. Analyses followed the DHS guidance on weighting and design-based estimation [@dhsguide2023] and used R 4.5.1 with `survey` 4.4.2, `tidyverse` 2.0.0, `flextable` 0.9.9 and `officer` 0.6.10 [@lumley2010]; scripts and session information are in the public repository.

## Ethical considerations

This study used de-identified secondary data from KDHS 2022, obtained from The DHS Program under an approved data request. The original survey was approved by the Kenya Medical Research Institute Scientific and Ethics Review Unit and the ICF Institutional Review Board. No new participant contact occurred and no additional ethical approval was required.

# Results

## Participant flow and sample characteristics

Of `r fmt_count(key_results$sample_flow$n[key_results$sample_flow$step == "Raw PR records"])` records in the PR file, `r fmt_count(key_results$sample_flow$n[2])` were adult usual residents with complete design variables, of whom `r fmt_count(key_results$sample_flow$n[3])` were in short-questionnaire households where the modules were not administered. The analytic base was `r fmt_count(key_results$sample_long_questionnaire)` adults in `r fmt_count(key_results$sample_households_long_questionnaire)` long-questionnaire households with complete WG-SS data (Table S1). Item missingness within that base was below 1% for every outcome and covariate (Table S2); adults excluded from the fully adjusted insurance model (`r fmt_count(key_results$inclusion_comparison$n[key_results$inclusion_comparison$included == 0])`, `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * key_results$inclusion_comparison$n[key_results$inclusion_comparison$included == 0] / key_results$sample_long_questionnaire)`) were similar in age to those included (mean `r sprintf("%.1f", key_results$inclusion_comparison$mean_age[key_results$inclusion_comparison$included == 0])` versus `r sprintf("%.1f", key_results$inclusion_comparison$mean_age[key_results$inclusion_comparison$included == 1])` years) but less often rural (`r sprintf("%.0f%%", key_results$inclusion_comparison$pct_rural[key_results$inclusion_comparison$included == 0])` versus `r sprintf("%.0f%%", key_results$inclusion_comparison$pct_rural[key_results$inclusion_comparison$included == 1])`).

`r fmt_inline_pct(key_results$any_functional_difficulty)` of adults reported any functional difficulty and `r fmt_inline_pct(key_results$wg_disability)` met the WG threshold. Adults at the threshold were much older than adults below it (mean age `r table1$WG_stat[table1$Characteristic == "Mean age, years (95% CI)"]` versus `r table1$NoWG_stat[table1$Characteristic == "Mean age, years (95% CI)"]` years), more often rural, and concentrated in the poorer quintiles (Table 1). That imbalance is the reason the disability contrasts below are reported under more than one adjustment set.

## Insurance coverage across the severity gradient

Unadjusted coverage fell across severity categories, from `r table2$AnyInsurance[table2$Characteristic == "  No functional difficulty"]` at no difficulty to `r table2$AnyInsurance[table2$Characteristic == "  Severe functional difficulty"]` at severe difficulty, with NHIF tracking any insurance closely at every level (Table 2, Figure 1). Tested directly rather than read off overlapping intervals, the gradient is a single step. Coverage at mild difficulty did not differ from coverage at no difficulty (`r fmt_severity("crude", "Mild vs no difficulty")`); the step from mild to moderate did (`r fmt_severity("crude", "Moderate vs mild")`); and the further step from moderate to severe did not (`r fmt_severity("crude", "Severe vs moderate")`). The design-based global test of severity was significant unadjusted (`r fmt_global("crude")`) and after adjustment for sex, age group and residence (`r fmt_global("confounder")`), but not after wealth and education were added (`r fmt_global("full")`), where every adjacent contrast was null (Table S3). The multi-domain alternative behaved the same way: relative to no domain at threshold, the fully adjusted uninsured APR was `r fmt_apr_row(key_results$domain_burden, "domain_burdenOne domain at threshold")` for one domain and `r fmt_apr_row(key_results$domain_burden, "domain_burdenTwo or more domains at threshold")` for two or more (global p = `r sprintf("%.2f", key_results$domain_burden_global$p_value)`).

Because NHIF accounted for most cover, private and community schemes did not offset the gradient at any severity level. Among adults at the WG threshold, coverage also varied by domain, from `r fmt_pct_ci(lowest_domain_coverage$any_insurance_est, lowest_domain_coverage$any_insurance_ci_low, lowest_domain_coverage$any_insurance_ci_high)` for communication difficulty to `r fmt_pct_ci(highest_domain_coverage$any_insurance_est, highest_domain_coverage$any_insurance_ci_low, highest_domain_coverage$any_insurance_ci_high)` for walking difficulty; these domain estimates are descriptive, non-mutually exclusive and were not contrasted formally.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-2
#| tbl-cap: "Weighted insurance coverage by Washington Group Short Set disability severity and functional domain, adults aged 18 years and above, KDHS 2022."
publication_flextable(
  table2,
  footer_lines = c(
    "Source: Kenya DHS 2022. Survey-weighted estimates with logit-transformed 95% confidence intervals.",
    "Domain rows are non-mutually exclusive and are restricted to adults meeting the WG disability threshold.",
    "Adjacent severity categories are contrasted formally in Table S3; the intervals in this table are not a test of the differences between rows."
  ),
  header_labels = table_specs$table2$header_labels
)
```

```{r}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path("..", "05_figures", "Figure1_Insurance_By_Disability_Severity.png"))
```

## The disability contrast under three adjustment sets

Adults at the WG threshold were more likely to be uninsured than adults below it, unadjusted (`r fmt_contrast_apr("uninsured", "crude")`) and after adjustment for sex, age group and residence (`r fmt_contrast_apr("uninsured", "confounder")`, a standardised difference of `r fmt_contrast_pp_plain("uninsured", "confounder")`). Adding wealth quintile and educational attainment removed the association (`r fmt_contrast_apr("uninsured", "full")`; standardised difference `r fmt_contrast_pp_plain("uninsured", "full")`). The crude coverage deficit is therefore accounted for, statistically, by the age and socioeconomic composition of the disability population, and specifically by wealth and education rather than by age: adjusting for age alone left the association intact.

The two utilisation contrasts behaved differently. Outpatient use in the previous four weeks was higher among adults at the threshold in every specification (crude `r fmt_contrast_apr_short("outpatient_last4w", "crude")`; confounder-adjusted `r fmt_contrast_apr_short("outpatient_last4w", "confounder")`; fully adjusted `r fmt_contrast_apr_short("outpatient_last4w", "full")`), as was hospitalisation in the previous 12 months (fully adjusted `r fmt_contrast_apr_short("inpatient_last12m", "full")`, a standardised difference of `r fmt_contrast_pp_plain("inpatient_last12m", "full")`). Table 3 and Figure 2 set the three outcomes side by side.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-3
#| tbl-cap: "Prevalence ratios and standardised prevalence differences for adults meeting the Washington Group Short Set disability threshold compared with adults below it, whole adult sample, KDHS 2022."
publication_flextable(
  table3,
  footer_lines = c(
    "Source: Kenya DHS 2022. Survey-weighted quasi-Poisson models with a log link; confidence limits use the survey degrees of freedom.",
    "Standardised differences are marginal contrasts in percentage points over the covariate distribution of the analytic sample, with delta-method confidence limits.",
    "Wealth and education are plausibly downstream of lifelong functional difficulty, so the third row of each block estimates an association net of that pathway rather than a more completely confounder-adjusted one."
  ),
  header_labels = table_specs$table3$header_labels
)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-2
#| fig-cap: "Prevalence ratios for adults at the Washington Group disability threshold versus adults below it, by adjustment set, KDHS 2022. Points show prevalence ratios and horizontal bars 95% confidence intervals on a log scale."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5.4
knitr::include_graphics(file.path("..", "05_figures", "Figure2_Disability_Contrast_By_Adjustment.png"))
```

## Service use and payment at outpatient contact

Outpatient use was `r fmt_inline_pct(key_results$disability_outpatient)` among adults at the WG threshold and `r fmt_inline_pct(key_results$no_disability_outpatient)` among adults below it; hospitalisation was `r fmt_inline_pct(key_results$disability_inpatient)` and `r fmt_inline_pct(key_results$no_disability_inpatient)` respectively (Table 4).

Among adults who used outpatient care, payment of some amount was close to universal: `r fmt_inline_pct(key_results$disability_payment)` of those with disability and `r fmt_inline_pct(key_results$no_disability_payment)` of those without. Within the disability group, payment incidence was `r fmt_inline_pct(key_results$disability_payment_insured)` among insured users and `r fmt_inline_pct(key_results$disability_payment_uninsured)` among uninsured users (Figure 3). In the whole-sample model among outpatient users, holding any insurance was not associated with a lower probability of paying (APR `r fmt_inline_apr(key_results$model_payment_whole, "insured_any")`; `r fmt_inline_p_clause(key_results$model_payment_whole, "insured_any")`). Because `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * key_results$payment_outcome_counts$weighted_paid)` of users paid something, this outcome has little room to discriminate, and these estimates condition on having sought care.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-4
#| tbl-cap: "Weighted service utilisation and payment at the last outpatient visit by disability status and insurance coverage, adults aged 18 years and above, KDHS 2022."
publication_flextable(
  table4,
  footer_lines = c(
    "Source: Kenya DHS 2022. Survey-weighted estimates; n is the unweighted denominator for the adjacent column.",
    "Utilisation is estimated among all adults in the row group; payment only among those who used outpatient care in the previous four weeks.",
    "Payment records whether any money was paid, not how much. Amounts and payers are in Table 5."
  ),
  header_labels = table_specs$table4$header_labels
)
```

Bars show survey-weighted proportions and error bars logit-transformed 95% confidence intervals; the shaded bar rests on fewer than 30 respondents."
```{r}
#| fig-width: 7

knitr::include_graphics(file.path("..", "05_figures", "Figure3_Outpatient_Payment_By_Severity_Insurance.png"))
```

## What was paid, and who paid it

The amount data locate the financial-protection question more precisely than the incidence data can (Table 5). Among `r fmt_count(key_results$cost_payers_n)` adults who paid and reported an amount, the median gross cost of the visit was `r fmt_money_row("WG disability, insured", "median")` KSh for insured adults with disability and `r fmt_money_row("WG disability, uninsured", "median")` KSh for uninsured adults with disability. The cash amount, the part met out of pocket, was `r fmt_money_row("WG disability, insured", "cash_median")` KSh and `r fmt_money_row("WG disability, uninsured", "cash_median")` KSh respectively. Adjusted for sex, age group, residence, wealth and education, adults with disability paid `r fmt_ratio_row(key_results$cost_model, "wg_disability")` times as much in gross terms as adults without disability (n = `r fmt_count(key_results$cost_model_n)`), and insured adults paid `r fmt_ratio_row(key_results$cost_model, "insured_any")` times as much as uninsured adults; on the cash amount the corresponding ratios were `r fmt_ratio_row(key_results$cash_model, "wg_disability")` and `r fmt_ratio_row(key_results$cash_model, "insured_any")`.

The payer split explains why holding cover changed so little. Among insured adults with disability who paid, an insurer met any part of the bill for `r fmt_pct_row(key_results$payer_source_summary, "WG disability, insured", "insurer")`, and the mean cash share of the reported amounts was `r fmt_pct_row(key_results$payer_source_summary, "WG disability, insured", "cash")`. Among all insured payers the insurer contribution was `r fmt_pct_row(key_results$payer_source_summary, "No WG disability, insured", "insurer")`. Among uninsured adults with disability, no respondent reported any insurer contribution, as expected.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-5
#| tbl-cap: "Amount paid at the last outpatient visit and the source of that payment, among adults who used outpatient care in the previous four weeks and reported paying, KDHS 2022."
publication_flextable(
  table5,
  footer_lines = c(
    "Source: Kenya DHS 2022. Survey-weighted estimates; amounts are Kenyan shillings at the time of the survey.",
    "Restricted to respondents who reported paying, which is the questionnaire's own skip pattern for these items. Estimates describe the size and source of a payment among those who made one.",
    "The amount is the gross cost of the visit (sh304); the cash figure is the part met out of pocket (sh305a). Insurer contribution is any non-zero amount met by NHIF or private insurance.",
    "KDHS does not collect household consumption, so catastrophic health expenditure cannot be constructed from these data."
  ),
  header_labels = table_specs$table6$header_labels
)
```

## Variation within the disability population

Within the population of adults at the WG threshold (`r fmt_count(key_results$uninsured_model_n)`), wealth dominated the adjusted model for uninsured status: compared with the richest quintile, uninsured prevalence was higher in the richer (APR `r fmt_inline_apr(key_results$model_uninsured, "wealthRicher")`), middle (`r fmt_inline_apr(key_results$model_uninsured, "wealthMiddle")`), poorer (`r fmt_inline_apr(key_results$model_uninsured, "wealthPoorer")`) and poorest (`r fmt_inline_apr(key_results$model_uninsured, "wealthPoorest")`) quintiles. Older age was associated with lower uninsured prevalence, and severe difficulty was not associated with higher uninsured prevalence than moderate difficulty (`r fmt_inline_apr(key_results$model_uninsured, "wg_severitySevere functional difficulty")`; `r fmt_inline_p_clause(key_results$model_uninsured, "wg_severitySevere functional difficulty")`). In the corresponding payment model among outpatient users with disability (`r fmt_count(key_results$payment_model_n)`), insurance was not associated with payment incidence (`r fmt_inline_apr(key_results$model_payment, "insured_any")`; `r fmt_inline_p_clause(key_results$model_payment, "insured_any")`). These are contrasts across prevalence-ratio scales within one subpopulation and are not comparable measures of importance across variables.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-6
#| tbl-cap: "Survey-weighted adjusted prevalence ratios for uninsured status and for any payment at the last outpatient visit within the population of adults meeting the Washington Group Short Set disability threshold, KDHS 2022."
publication_flextable(
  table6,
  footer_lines = c(
    "Source: Kenya DHS 2022. Survey-weighted quasi-Poisson models with a log link; confidence limits use the survey degrees of freedom.",
    "These models describe variation within the disability subpopulation; the disability contrast itself is in Table 3.",
    "The payment model conditions on having used outpatient care, which is itself associated with disability, insurance and wealth, so its estimates are descriptive associations among users."
  ),
  header_labels = table_specs$table5$header_labels
)
```

## Sensitivity analyses

Grouping "don't know" insurance responses with the uninsured left both the confounder-adjusted (`r fmt_apr_row(key_results$sensitivity_dk %>% dplyr::filter(specification == "confounder"), "wg_disability")`) and the fully adjusted (`r fmt_apr_row(key_results$sensitivity_dk %>% dplyr::filter(specification == "full"), "wg_disability")`) disability contrasts unchanged. The domain-count specification of disability burden gave the same null after full adjustment as the severity summary. Adults excluded from the fully adjusted model for missing covariates differed little from those included.

# Discussion

## Principal findings

Four findings stand, and the differences between them matter more than any one of them.

First, the crude coverage deficit among adults with disability is real as a description and does not survive adjustment for wealth and education. Uninsured prevalence was higher at the WG threshold unadjusted and after adjustment for sex, age group and residence, a standardised difference of about `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * key_results$contrast("uninsured", "confounder")$standardised_difference)` percentage points, and the association disappeared when wealth and education entered the model. Because those two variables are plausibly consequences of lifelong functional difficulty rather than causes of it, the honest reading is not that disability is irrelevant to coverage but that its association with coverage operates through economic position. Adjusting for age alone did not weaken the association, which rules out the simplest alternative explanation.

Second, the severity pattern is a single step, not a slope, and it is a compositional step. The only adjacent contrast that reached significance was mild to moderate, and no contrast survived adjustment for wealth and education. The earlier reading of these data as showing a severity threshold at which the financing system fails is not supported by a formal test.

Third, adults with disability used more care, and this contrast survived every specification: about 63% higher outpatient use and about twice the hospitalisation prevalence after full adjustment. Greater need is not explained away by composition in the way that lower coverage is.

Fourth, at the point of care, insurance rarely paid. Nearly every outpatient user paid something regardless of cover, and among insured adults with disability who paid, an insurer met any part of the bill in roughly one case in seven. Insured adults with disability also paid larger amounts, both gross and in cash, which is consistent with insured users reaching higher-level or costlier providers rather than with cover reducing what they pay there.

## Relation to existing evidence

The socioeconomic patterning of coverage reproduces what earlier Kenyan and cross-country analyses have found [@kimani2014; @kazungu2017; @barasa2021; @alhajeri2026]. The contribution here is the disability stratification and the joint treatment of coverage, use and payment in one adult sample, not the discovery that coverage is pro-rich.

The payment results should be read alongside the coarsened exact matching analysis of the same survey, which found that insured people had substantially higher gross expenditure but lower net out-of-pocket payment after reimbursement was taken into account [@okova2026]. Our gross finding agrees with theirs. Our net finding does not point the same way: conditional on having paid, and adjusted for socioeconomic position, insured adults still reported larger cash amounts. The two analyses answer different questions, ours conditional on a payment having been made and theirs on matched samples including those who paid nothing, so they are complementary rather than contradictory, and the divergence marks where more work is needed. What both establish is that an insurance indicator and a payment indicator are not substitutes for one another.

The qualitative finding that Kenyan pro-poor financing schemes can enrol poor women with disabilities and still leave them paying at the facility [@kabia2018] is reproduced here at national scale and with an amount attached. It also sits within a longer Kenyan record of NHIF membership delivering incomplete financial protection and uneven benefit access, documented in the fund's own reform history [@barasa2018], in analyses of coverage and out-of-pocket costs among chronically ill and older populations [@mbau2020; @oyando2023], and in facility-level work on medicine availability and chronic-care readiness [@otieno2023]. Our payer split gives that record a mechanism at the point of contact: for most insured users who paid, the scheme contributed nothing to the bill in front of them.

## Implications for the SHA transition

The Social Health Insurance Act 2023 routes support for people who cannot pay through means testing of the household, not through a disability category [@kenya2023sha; @kenya2024shiregs]. Our results are consistent with that design in one respect and awkward for it in another. They are consistent with it in that the coverage deficit associated with disability runs through household economic position, which is what a means-tested premium subsidy targets. They are awkward for it in that the WG-SS threshold, the instrument used to identify disability in population surveys, is not the instrument used to identify eligibility administratively, and KDHS records neither certification under the Persons with Disabilities Act nor programme enrolment [@kenya2025pda]. Nothing in these data indicates how many adults with functional difficulty would be identified by a means test, and no inference of that kind should be drawn from a WG-SS category.

The payment results carry a sharper implication. A subsidy that covers a premium addresses the enrolment margin. It does not, on this evidence, address the payment margin, where holding cover was associated with neither a lower probability of paying nor a smaller amount paid. A monitoring framework built on enrolment counts would record a transition from uninsured to enrolled as a success while the household's outlay at the next outpatient visit stayed where it was. Monitoring should therefore track the amount paid and the payer split, both of which KDHS already collects, and not enrolment alone.

For rehabilitation and assistive services specifically, these data are silent: KDHS 2022 does not record rehabilitation contacts, assistive product access or therapy costs. What the data do show is that the point-of-care payment barrier that would apply to such services was substantial and was not removed by cover. Establishing whether rehabilitation access moves with the SHA benefit package will require a survey instrument that asks about it.

## Strengths and limitations

The strengths are the national sampling frame, the design-based analysis throughout, the use of the WG-SS as the organising equity dimension, and the availability of coverage, use, amount and payer in one consistent adult sample.

The limitations are substantial and shape what can be concluded. The design is cross-sectional, with exposure and outcome measured at the same moment, so no causal claim is made. The data are household-reported and largely proxy-reported, which is likely to matter most for the cognition and communication domains, for less visible difficulty, and for another member's insurance status; the file does not identify which member responded. Wealth and education may be mediators, and if they are, the fully adjusted estimates are not the estimates of interest for a total association; both are reported for that reason. Two analyses condition on care-seeking or on having paid, which can induce selection bias, and neither is interpretable as an effect of insurance. The amount items are asked only of those who paid, so nothing here describes the cost faced by people who did not seek care or who were turned away. KDHS collects no consumption or income measure, so catastrophic and impoverishing expenditure cannot be constructed. Severity is a maximum across domains rather than a validated scale, although the domain-count alternative gave the same answer. Some cells are small, notably insured adults with severe difficulty (n = 19), and are marked in the figures rather than interpreted. Analyses are complete-case, though missingness was under 1%. The modules were administered in half of sampled households, so estimates generalise to adult usual residents represented by that half-sample design, and not to institutionalised populations, people absent from households, or those whose disability prevented reliable proxy report. Finally, the WG-SS threshold is not Kenyan administrative disability certification, and the two should not be treated as interchangeable.

# Conclusions

Immediately before the SHA transition, Kenyan adults with disability were less likely to hold insurance, used substantially more outpatient and inpatient care, and paid at the point of care about as often as everyone else. The coverage gap was explained statistically by their older, poorer and less educated composition; the higher use of care was not, and neither was the payment burden. Among insured adults with disability who paid, an insurer met part of the bill in roughly one case in seven.

Two things follow for monitoring the transition. Enrolment counts will not reveal whether the financing system has begun to work for this population, because enrolment was not what distinguished payers from non-payers. And a disability-specific coverage target may be the wrong instrument if the coverage deficit runs through household poverty, which the Act already means-tests for; the test of the reform is whether the amount paid at the point of care falls, which KDHS is already equipped to measure.
